cards.text: Pull up a stool, friend, because this is the account of Isaac, Abraham's son. At forty years old, Isaac marries Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean from Paddan-aram and the sister of Laban the Aramean. That's a whole family tree in one breath, and I need a nap just from READING it.
Later, Rebekah is barren, so Isaac takes it straight to the LORD in prayer for his wife. I bet those were some heavy prayers.

cards.question: Isaac prays to the LORD for Rebekah because she can't have children. How does the LORD answer?

answers.text: He tells Isaac to keep waiting
He sends an angel with a sign

cards.text: But the children inside her struggle with each other, and Rebekah says, “Why is this happening to me?” Friend, they haven't even been BORN yet and they're already fighting over the armrest.

cards.question: Rebekah's children are struggling inside her, and she wants answers. What does she do?

answers.text: She goes to inquire of the LORD
She asks Isaac to pray again
She goes back to her family

cards.question: Rebekah goes to the LORD, and He answers her. What does He say is in her womb?
The LORD also tells Rebekah that one people will be stronger than the other, and the younger will serve the older.

cards.text: When her time comes, sure enough, it's TWINS! The first one comes out red, covered with hair like a fur coat, so they name him Esau.

cards.question: Right after Esau comes his twin brother. How does the second twin come out?

cards.text: So the heel-grabber gets named Jacob, and Isaac is sixty years old when the twins are born. Married at forty, twins at sixty: that's TWENTY years, friend, and I used to complain about a twelve-minute oven timer.
The boys grow up, and these two may share a birthday, but they do NOT share a personality. Same oven, same batch, two completely different cookies.

cards.question: Esau, the red and hairy twin, grows up. What kind of man does he become?
Esau's twin, Jacob, grows up to be a quiet man who stays at home.

cards.text: Now, Isaac has a taste for wild game. And in this family, that's about to matter.

cards.question: Isaac has a taste for wild game, so Isaac loved ___, but Rebekah loved ___.

cards.text: One day Jacob's cooking some stew when Esau comes in from the field famished. And I mean FAMISHED, like me at three in the afternoon on a day I skipped the cookie dough.
Esau says to Jacob, “Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am famished.” I bet he never even asked what was in it. He just saw RED.

cards.question: Because of that red stew, Esau ends up with another name. What is it?
Esau is famished and asking Jacob for stew. What does Jacob want from Esau first?
Jacob wants Esau's birthright before he hands over any stew. What does Esau say back?

answers.text: He's about to die so what good is it
Their father will never allow it
He'll just buy it back tomorrow

cards.question: Esau's ready to give up his birthright for the stew. What does Jacob make him do first?

cards.text: So Jacob gives Esau some bread and lentil stew, and Esau eats and drinks, then gets up and goes away. Friend, I've seen people think harder about a parking spot.

cards.question: Esau eats, drinks, gets up and goes away. How does the passage sum it up? Thus Esau ___ his birthright.

cards.text: Esau's full, Jacob's holding the birthright, and this family? Oh, they're just getting WARMED UP. Keep your apron on, friend.

findings.problem: The joke 'That's a whole family tree in one breath, and I need a nap just from READING it' makes the wording of Genesis 25:19-20 the target. It treats Scripture as tiring to read. It should be self-deprecating about Papa Dorin, not about the text.

rule.text: His humor never targets God, Jesus, Scripture or the Marriage Supper.

findings.problem: 'Later, Rebekah is barren' moves 'Later' onto her barrenness, which reads as if she only became barren later. In Genesis 25:21, 'Later' goes with Isaac's prayer: 'Later, Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren.'

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The card states 'Married at forty', which comes from Genesis 25:20, but it cites only Genesis 25:26. The citation should cover every verse the card uses.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: 'He just saw RED' puns on the idiom 'see red', which means getting angry. Esau is famished, not angry (Genesis 25:30), so the comparison doesn't share the core action and won't click.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: 'Esau's full, Jacob's holding the birthright' recaps what cards 12 and 13 already told and adds nothing from Genesis 25:34. Since verse 34 is asked on card 13, this card should be just the line that says the story isn't over.
